newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Coalition woes deter more Khmer defections - rebels.
newsitem.headline: Coalition woes deter more Khmer defections - rebels.

text.p: Khmer Rouge hard-liners in northern Cambodia are considering defecting to the government but are deterred by tension between the two main coalition parties, rebel defectors said on Saturday.

Khmer Rouge defectors from this former rebel base on northwest Cambodia's border with Thailand said they had sent colleagues to the hard-liners' Anlong Veng camp to try to persuade them to come over to the government.

"I think it won't be long, I can't say when, before the whole of Anlong Veng falls to the government but now they (hard-liners) said they were focusing on (problems between) the two big political parties," an officer of the defectors said.

Ieng Vudh, son of Ieng Sary, leader of the defectors, confirmed they were trying to woo their former colleagues, and said: "The main thing is that the two big political parties in the government must have real unity."

Cambodian People's Party of Second Prime Minister Hun Sen and First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh's royalist FUNCINPEC party, formed an uneasy coalition to avoid renewed war after U.N.-run polls in 1993.

Relations soured when Ranariddh asked for a larger share of power last March. They united in August to persuade thousands of Khmer Rouge fighters to defect but tensions returned as the two leaders vied to win the allegiance of the rebels.
Hun Sen made his first visit to Phnom Malai on Saturday, flying in with officials, diplomats and journalists to launch a polio eradication programme among the children of the Khmer Rouge.
"Before we used weapons to fight each other, but now we use medicine to fight disease," the co-premier said.

Hun Sen played a key role in winning a royal pardon last year for Ieng Sary from a 1979 death sentence handed down in absentia for his role in the killing of more than one million people during the 1975-79 Khmer Rouge regime, when he was foreign minister.
Ieng Sary, who was on hand to greet Hun Sen, has since come over to the government but has refused, at least publicly, to side with rival alliances being formed by the two premiers.
More than 10,000 Khmer Rouge guerrillas have defected to the government leaving a core of about 2,000 hard-liners around the northern Cambodian base of Anlong Veng.

The Khmer Rouge, whose rule left more than one million people dead from execution, starvation, disease and overwork, reneged on a U.N.-brokered peace pact and has been fighting the coalition government formed after 1993 polls.
